opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core intuition is that features, in the way we've traditionally talked about them, are really a property of the activations. You look at a particular layer, you look at the activation space, and you ask: what directions in this space are meaningful? That's been a really productive frame. Sparse dictionary learning, SAEs, transcoders, all of that comes out of it. But I've increasingly felt it's a bit like trying to understand a program by looking only at the values of its variables at particular moments, rather than at the code itself.

The network doesn't really care about activations for their own sake. Activations are what you get when the network's *mechanisms*, the computations implemented in its parameters, act on a particular input. So if you want the fundamental units, I think it makes more sense to look for them in the parameters, in the computations, and then treat the features you see in activations as a kind of downstream shadow of those computations.

That framing helps a lot with the cases that have been awkward for the activation-centric view. Take multidimensional features. There's good evidence that some things networks represent aren't single directions but subspaces or manifolds, like the circular representations of days of the week or months of the year. If your basic unit is "one direction in activation space," you have to do a lot of post-hoc work to stitch those back together. But if you ask "what's the computation here?", it's natural that one mechanism might read from or write to a multidimensional subspace. The dimensionality just falls out of what the mechanism does. You don't have to decide in advance that everything is one-dimensional.

Multilayer features are similar. A lot of what networks do isn't localized to a single layer. Something might get computed partly in one layer and partly in the next, or be spread across several attention heads and MLPs. If you analyze each layer separately, you end up with features in layer 5 and features in layer 6 and then a hard problem of figuring out how they relate, and you can get artifacts, like feature splitting or features that exist only because of where you happened to cut the network. Thinking in terms of computations lets you say: this mechanism spans these parameters across these layers, and that's the natural unit. Layer boundaries are an architectural convenience, not necessarily where the conceptual boundaries are.

There's also a more philosophical point about what we're trying to get out of interpretability. Ultimately we want to explain the network's behavior, and behavior is caused by computation. So a description in terms of computations is closer to what we care about. The approach my collaborators and I have been working on, parameter decomposition, tries to break a network's weights into components that are each simple, that each matter only for a small fraction of inputs, and that together faithfully reconstruct the original network. If you get that right, multidimensional and multilayer structure isn't a special case you bolt on. It's just what some components look like.

I'll be honest that this is still early, and there are real open questions about scaling these methods and about whether we're carving the network at the right joints. But as a starting point, computations feel more fundamental to me than activations, and I think a lot of the puzzles that have shown up with SAEs get easier once you change that starting point.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to put it is that "feature" was always a proxy. When people started doing mechanistic interpretability, the thing we actually cared about was: what is this network doing? What's the algorithm? But algorithms are hard to see directly, so we reached for the nearest handle we could grab, which was representations. Directions in activation space. And that gave us a lot. Sparse autoencoders, dictionary learning, all of that is downstream of the idea that if you find the right basis for the activations, the computation will be legible in it.

But the trouble is that activations are only half the story. A representation is only meaningful because of what the network does with it downstream and what produced it upstream. So when you try to decompose activations in isolation, layer by layer, you run into these problems that I think are really symptomatic of having picked the wrong unit of analysis. You get feature splitting, where one concept fractures into a bunch of near-duplicates depending on dictionary size. You get features that look multidimensional, like the circular representations of days of the week or months, and it's not clear whether that's one feature or seven. And you get the cross-layer problem, where the same thing is being computed over several layers but your decomposition is forced to chop it up at each residual stream.

If you start from computations instead, a lot of that just dissolves. A computation is a piece of the network's parameters, a direction or a low-rank chunk of weights, that reads something in and writes something out. And the natural question becomes: what's the minimal set of such mechanisms that explains the network's behavior on each input? That's what we were going for with attribution-based parameter decomposition, and now with the stochastic parameter decomposition work. You're decomposing the weights, not the activations, and you're asking for the decomposition to be faithful, minimal, and simple.

What's nice is that multidimensionality falls out for free. If the network uses a three-dimensional subspace to do one thing, then the mechanism that implements it is just a rank-three object. You don't have to agonize over whether it's one feature or three, because the computation tells you. Same with multilayer structure. If a single mechanism spans the MLP in layer four and an attention head in layer seven, that's just a component whose parameters live in both places. There's no reason the units of the network's algorithm should line up with the layer boundaries we drew for engineering convenience.

And honestly I think there's a deeper point here, which is that the notion of a feature was borrowed from a picture where representations are primary and computation is what you infer from them. I'd flip that. The thing that's actually invariant, the thing the network was optimized to have, is the computation. Representations are an artifact of how that computation happens to be laid out. So if you want a decomposition that's principled rather than just empirically convenient, I think you have to ground it in the parameters, because that's where the algorithm literally lives.

astra-6.text:
I think computations are a useful starting point because, ultimately, we want to understand what the network is doing. Features are part of that story, but if we start by assuming that a feature is a direction in activation space, we’ve already made quite a strong assumption about how the network represents things.

A computation might involve several quantities that only really make sense together. So the natural unit of explanation could be a multidimensional space rather than a single direction. And that computation might unfold across several layers: one layer produces an intermediate result, another transforms it, and a later layer uses it. If we look at each layer independently, we can miss that continuity.

So I’d like to start by asking, ‘What computation is happening here, and what representations does it need?’ Then we can ask whether those representations are one-dimensional or multidimensional, and how they’re carried across layers. That makes the geometry something we’re trying to discover, rather than something we impose at the outset.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that features are useful to a network because of the computations they enable. If we start by assuming that a feature is a direction in activation space, we’ve already made a fairly strong assumption about how the network represents things. And that might cause us to miss structures that need several dimensions to describe, or that only really make sense when you look across multiple layers.

So I’d rather start by asking: what computation is the network doing, and what information does it need to carry out that computation? Then we can ask how that information is represented. A multidimensional feature might be several quantities that the network operates on together. And across layers, what we call different features might actually be different stages of the same computation.

That gives us a way to decide which structures matter beyond just whether they show up in a particular decomposition of the activations. We want to understand what role they play in producing the network’s behavior.

r001.rationale: It says multidimensional features can consist of several quantities the network operates on together, connecting their structure to the computations they enable.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss the transformer residual stream or computations spanning layers.
